blocks.text: A 44-year-old man has had a freckle on his upper back for years. His wife, who looks at his back more often than he does, says it has become darker and bigger over the last few months and bled once when he towelled himself. He is not worried. You are, because the single most important prognostic fact about this lesion is how deep it has grown, and that is decided by how quickly it is removed.

blocks.markdown: **Skin cancer** is the commonest cancer in fair-skinned populations. The main risk factor is ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure, particularly intermittent intense exposure and sunburn in childhood for melanoma, and cumulative exposure for squamous cell carcinoma. Other risks are fair skin and many naevi, a family history, immunosuppression (for example after organ transplantation) and previous skin cancer. The three tumours you must distinguish are **basal cell carcinoma (BCC)**, **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)** and **melanoma**. A second part of this unit concerns two dermatological emergencies, **Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)** with toxic epidermal necrolysis and **erythroderma**, in which the skin itself is failing.

blocks.title: The ABCDE assessment of a pigmented lesion
blocks.text: **A**symmetry (the two halves do not match), **B**order irregularity, **C**olour variation (several shades of brown, black, red, white or blue), **D**iameter (often over 6 mm, though melanomas can be smaller) and **E**volution (change in size, shape, colour, or new symptoms such as itch or bleeding). **Evolution** is the single most important feature, and the 'ugly duckling' sign (a lesion that looks different from the person's other moles) adds weight. The UK also uses the weighted seven-point checklist; any suspicious lesion is referred urgently for dermatological assessment.

blocks.markdown: **Melanoma** arises from melanocytes. It may develop in an existing naevus or de novo. Subtypes include **superficial spreading** (commonest, with a radial growth phase), **nodular** (rapid vertical growth, may be amelanotic and lack ABCDE features), **lentigo maligna** (on chronically sun-damaged skin of older people) and **acral lentiginous** (palms, soles and under nails). The most important prognostic factor is **Breslow thickness** (depth of invasion in millimetres from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell). A suspected melanoma should be removed by **excision biopsy with a small peripheral margin** rather than incisional biopsy or shave, so the full thickness can be measured; wider re-excision margins are then planned from the Breslow thickness according to current guidance. Suspected melanoma is referred under the urgent suspected cancer pathway.

blocks.title: Applying ABCDE
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old woman has a 9 mm brown-black pigmented lesion on her calf. One half is darker than the other, the border is notched, it contains brown, black and pink areas, and she says it has grown over the last 4 months. Apply ABCDE and decide what to do.

steps.text: Asymmetry: the halves differ in darkness, so A is positive.
Border: notched and irregular, so B is positive.
Colour: three shades (brown, black, pink), so C is positive.
Diameter: 9 mm, over 6 mm, so D is positive. Evolution: growth over 4 months is the most important feature, so E is positive.

All five criteria are positive, so this is a suspected melanoma. Arrange urgent referral on the suspected cancer pathway for dermatology review and excision biopsy with a narrow margin; do not shave or partially biopsy it in primary care.

blocks.answer: Five of five ABCDE features positive: suspected melanoma; urgent referral and complete excision biopsy.

blocks.caption: Comparison of the three main skin cancers (follow current NICE and BAD guidance).

blocks.markdown: **SCC and BCC in practice.** Keratinocyte cancers are usually treated by surgical excision. High-risk SCC features include size over 2 cm, thickness, perineural invasion, site on the lip or ear, and immunosuppression. Organ-transplant recipients have a markedly increased risk of SCC and need skin surveillance and sun protection advice. Pre-malignant **actinic keratoses** (rough scaly patches on sun-damaged skin) are treated with field therapy or cryotherapy. Prevention uses sun avoidance, protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen.

**Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)** form a spectrum of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, usually drug-induced, in which keratinocyte death causes epidermal detachment and mucosal erosions. Typical culprits are allopurinol, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin), sulfonamide antibiotics and nevirapine, 1 to 3 weeks after starting. A fever and flu-like prodrome is followed by painful dusky or target-like macules, blisters and erosions of the **mouth, eyes and genitals**; the **Nikolsky sign** (shearing off the epidermis with lateral pressure) may be positive. Severity is defined by the percentage of body surface area (BSA) with detachment.

blocks.caption: Classification by percentage of body surface area with epidermal detachment. In the rule of nines, each arm is 9 percent, each leg 18 percent, the anterior trunk 18 percent, and the head 9 percent.

blocks.title: Classifying epidermal detachment
blocks.prompt: A patient 12 days after starting a new antiepileptic has epidermal detachment over the whole anterior trunk and one whole arm. Classify the reaction and outline the first steps.

steps.text: Using the rule of nines: anterior trunk is 18 percent and one arm is 9 percent.
27 percent lies between 10 and 30 percent, so this is SJS/TEN overlap, which is managed as a medical emergency.

First steps: stop the suspected culprit drug immediately, admit to a burns unit or intensive care for specialist dermatology care, give fluids and analgesia, protect the eyes (ophthalmology review), care for mucosae, monitor for infection, and discuss immunomodulatory therapy with a specialist. Record the drug allergy.

blocks.answer: 27 percent BSA detachment: SJS/TEN overlap; stop the culprit drug and give emergency supportive care.

blocks.markdown: **Erythroderma** is generalised erythema affecting more than 90 percent of the body surface, usually with scaling. Causes include exacerbation of eczema or psoriasis, drug reactions, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and idiopathic disease. The skin loses its barrier and thermoregulatory functions, so patients develop **fluid and protein loss, heat loss (hypothermia) or rigors, tachycardia and high-output cardiac failure, and infection**. It is an emergency requiring admission, warm environment, fluid and nutritional support, emollients, treatment of any identified cause, and review of all drugs. Abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids or methotrexate in psoriasis can precipitate it.

blocks.title: Two rules
blocks.text: A pigmented lesion that is changing must be excised completely, not partially biopsied or shaved; the Breslow thickness cannot be measured from a partial specimen. A patient who develops fever, mucosal erosions and a spreading painful rash after starting a new drug has SJS/TEN until proven otherwise; stop the drug and admit.

points: ABCDE (asymmetry, border, colour, diameter, evolution) identifies suspicious pigmented lesions; evolution is the strongest feature, and suspected melanoma is excised completely and referred urgently, with Breslow thickness guiding management.

BCC is a slow, locally invasive pearly rolled-edge nodule, SCC is a scaly or ulcerated nodule with metastatic potential (especially in the immunosuppressed), and melanoma is the aggressive melanocytic cancer.

SJS/TEN (drug-induced mucosal erosions with epidermal detachment, classified by percentage BSA) and erythroderma (over 90 percent erythema with barrier and thermoregulatory failure) are emergencies needing admission, supportive care and cause removal.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 5 mm pigmented lesion on her thigh that was stable for years but over the last 3 months has become darker and itchy. She has no other concerning moles. Which feature is the most important reason to refer urgently?

options.text: Evolution: recent change in colour with new itch
The lesion is on a covered site

questions.correctOptionText: Evolution: recent change in colour with new itch

distractorRationale.a: Small diameter does not exclude melanoma.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: change over time is the strongest predictor of melanoma.
distractorRationale.c: Age does not rule out melanoma.
distractorRationale.d: Covered sites are also relevant but do not provide reassurance.

questions.explanation: Evolution of a lesion (change in size, shape, colour or new symptoms) is the single most important feature. A small diameter does not exclude melanoma, so this lesion should be referred urgently for dermatological assessment.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old retired fisherman has a 1 cm slowly enlarging nodule on the side of his nose. It has a pearly translucent rim, fine surface blood vessels and a central crusted ulcer. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pearly, rolled edge, telangiectasia and central ulcer on the face are typical of BCC.
distractorRationale.b: Melanoma usually shows pigment or rapid vertical growth and irregular colour.
distractorRationale.c: Seborrhoeic keratoses are waxy, stuck-on lesions without ulceration.
distractorRationale.d: Actinic keratoses are flat or slightly raised rough scaly patches.

questions.explanation: BCC classically presents on the face with a pearly, translucent, telangiectatic border and may ulcerate. It grows slowly and invades locally but rarely metastasises, and is treated by excision or alternative local therapy.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 8 years ago and takes long-term immunosuppression presents with a 1.5 cm firm, crusted, rapidly growing nodule on the helix of his ear. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is most likely a BCC and metastasis is almost never seen
It is likely an SCC; the immunosuppression and site (ear) raise the risk of recurrence and metastasis, so urgent excision is needed
It is a benign sebaceous cyst
It can be monitored in 6 months

questions.correctOptionText: It is likely an SCC; the immunosuppression and site (ear) raise the risk of recurrence and metastasis, so urgent excision is needed

distractorRationale.a: BCC is more likely pearly and rarely metastasises, but SCC is more common in transplant recipients.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: SCC risk is raised in transplant recipients and ear and lip tumours have higher metastatic potential.
distractorRationale.c: A rapidly growing crusted nodule is not a benign cyst.

questions.explanation: Immunosuppression, especially after organ transplantation, greatly increases the incidence and aggressiveness of SCC. Lesions on the ear or lip carry higher metastatic risk, so prompt excision and surveillance are required.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman started lamotrigine 3 weeks ago. She now has fever, painful mouth and eye erosions, and a spreading rash of dusky target-like lesions with some blistering. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue lamotrigine and add oral antihistamine
Stop lamotrigine and admit urgently for specialist supportive care
Apply emollient and review in one week

questions.correctOptionText: Stop lamotrigine and admit urgently for specialist supportive care

distractorRationale.a: Continuing the culprit drug can be fatal.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: this is suspected SJS/TEN; stop the drug and admit for supportive care.
distractorRationale.c: Delaying review risks progression of detachment and sepsis.
distractorRationale.d: Increasing the dose worsens the reaction.

questions.explanation: The timing, mucosal erosions and target-like blistering rash after starting an anticonvulsant are classic for SJS/TEN. The culprit drug must be stopped immediately and the patient admitted for specialist supportive care, usually in a burns or intensive care setting.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing psoriasis stopped his treatment abruptly and now has generalised redness and scaling over 95 percent of his skin. He is shivering, has a heart rate of 124 and his temperature is 35.8 C. Which complication explains the shivering and low temperature?

options.text: Loss of thermoregulatory function due to widespread skin vasodilation and barrier failure

questions.correctOptionText: Loss of thermoregulatory function due to widespread skin vasodilation and barrier failure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: erythroderma causes heat loss, fluid loss and high cardiac output.
distractorRationale.b: Eye infection does not explain generalised thermoregulatory failure.
distractorRationale.d: Hyperglycaemia is not the cause of shivering and hypothermia here.

questions.explanation: In erythroderma, widespread vasodilation and loss of the skin barrier cause heat and fluid loss, hypothermia and high-output cardiac strain. Patients need admission, warmth, fluids, emollients and identification of the underlying cause.

questions.stem: A pigmented lesion with a diameter of less than 6 mm cannot be a melanoma.
questions.explanation: Diameter over 6 mm is only one of the ABCDE features. Small melanomas exist, and evolution and other features are more important than size alone.

questions.stem: A patient with SJS/TEN has epidermal detachment over both entire legs. Using the rule of nines (each leg 18 percent of body surface area), what percentage of body surface area is detached?
questions.explanation: Both legs: $18\% + 18\% = 36\%$. Detachment of more than 30 percent of body surface area classifies the reaction as toxic epidermal necrolysis, which carries a high mortality and needs intensive supportive care.

questions.stem: Explain how you would assess a pigmented lesion using ABCDE and describe the appropriate management of a suspected melanoma, including why partial biopsy is avoided.
markingGuide: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolution
Evolution is the most important; the ugly duckling sign adds weight; amelanotic and nodular melanoma may lack typical features
Urgent suspected cancer referral to dermatology
Complete excision biopsy with a narrow margin
Partial biopsy or shave prevents accurate Breslow thickness measurement and may compromise staging
Breslow thickness guides wider re-excision margins and further staging
questions.explanation: The ABCDE approach structures risk assessment. Breslow thickness is the key prognostic measure, so complete excision is needed to measure it accurately.

questions.stem: Distinguish basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma by appearance, site, behaviour and principal treatment.
markingGuide: BCC: pearly translucent nodule, rolled edge, telangiectasia, face, slow, locally invasive, rarely metastasises; excision or Mohs
SCC: firm scaly or crusted nodule/ulcer on sun-exposed skin, may arise from actinic keratosis; can metastasise, higher risk with immunosuppression, ear or lip; excision with margin
Melanoma: pigmented asymmetric lesion with colour variation (or amelanotic nodule), aggressive, metastasises early; wide excision guided by Breslow thickness and further therapy if advanced
Risk factors: UV exposure, fair skin, immunosuppression
questions.explanation: The three tumours differ in their cell of origin, appearance and metastatic potential, which drives urgency of referral and extent of surgery.

questions.stem: Describe the features of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis and erythroderma, and explain why each is a dermatological emergency.
markingGuide: SJS/TEN: drug-induced, 1 to 3 weeks after exposure; fever prodrome; painful dusky or target-like macules, blistering, Nikolsky sign; erosions of mouth, eyes, genitals
Classification by percentage BSA detached (SJS under 10, overlap 10 to 30, TEN over 30)
Emergency: skin failure, fluid and protein loss, sepsis, eye and mucosal scarring; stop culprit drug, supportive care in burns or intensive care, ophthalmology input
Erythroderma: over 90 percent BSA erythema and scaling; causes include eczema, psoriasis, drugs, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Complications: fluid and protein loss, thermoregulatory failure, high-output cardiac failure, infection
Management: admit, warmth, fluids, emollients, treat cause, review drugs
questions.explanation: Both conditions involve failure of the skin's barrier and homeostatic functions, so complications are systemic and life-threatening, and management is supportive plus removal of the cause.
